title: A Uganda Family Safari for Several Households Works Best When the Ages Set the Plan
meta_title: Uganda Family Safari, Shared by Several Families
meta_description: Planning a Uganda family safari for several households? Age rules, a mixed-age route, vehicles, rooms and permit costs, from our Nairobi team.
excerpt: A Uganda family safari for several households works when ages drive the plan: gorillas from 15, chimpanzees from 12, one vehicle per family and two nights in Bwindi.
content:
A Uganda family safari for several households usually means seven to ten days through Kibale Forest, Queen Elizabeth National Park and Bwindi, timed around one rule: gorilla trekking starts at 15 and chimpanzee tracking at 12. Plan the route, vehicles and rooms around everyone's ages first, and the rest falls into place.

Organising a trip for your own family is one thing. Organising it for your sister's family, the grandparents and a friend's teenagers is another, with different budgets, energy levels and permits to juggle. This guide is written for the person holding that spreadsheet. It covers who can do what, a route that suits mixed ages, how to split vehicles and rooms, what the fixed fees add up to, and the paperwork. For the wider picture of how we run a Uganda family safari and other trips for relatives and friends, see our family group safaris page.

Quick Facts

  • Classic family route: Entebbe, Kibale Forest, Queen Elizabeth National Park, Bwindi, back to Entebbe (7-10 days)
  • Age rules: Gorilla trekking 15+, chimpanzee tracking 12+ (Uganda Wildlife Authority)
  • Gorilla permit: US$800 per eligible person, chimpanzee permit in Kibale US$250 (UWA tariff for Jan 2027-June 2028, checked November 2026)
  • Child park entry: Children aged 5-15 pay a reduced rate; under-5s enter free
  • Best months: June-August and December-February (driest, school holidays)
  • Group size per gorilla family: 8 visitors a day, so larger parties are split
  • Getting around: 4x4 safari vehicles seating six to seven, or domestic flights for the long Bwindi leg

What Makes a Uganda Family Safari Different From Kenya or Tanzania?

A Uganda family safari is built around forests and primates rather than open-plains game drives alone. You still see elephants, buffalo, hippos and lions, but the headline moments happen on foot, with rangers, in Kibale and Bwindi. That changes how you plan for children.

On a Kenya or Tanzania safari, a five-year-old and a grandparent can share almost every activity from the vehicle. In Uganda the age limits split the group on at least two days, so the trip needs a plan for those who stay behind. The upside of a Uganda family safari is variety: a boat on the Kazinga Channel, a wetland boardwalk, tree-climbing lions in Ishasha and a forest full of monkeys keep teenagers more engaged than a week of game drives. If you are still choosing the country, our Kenya vs Uganda safari comparison sets out the trade-offs.

A Uganda family safari also rewards a slower pace. Distances between parks are real, roads can be rough, and the best lodges are small. A family group that accepts one full travel day in every three gets far more out of the trip than one that tries to add Murchison Falls and Lake Mburo to the same week.

Who Can Do What? Age Limits and Activity Fees

The Uganda Wildlife Authority sets a minimum age of 15 for gorilla trekking and 12 for chimpanzee tracking, and rangers check. Most other activities, including game drives, launch cruises and community visits, have no formal age limit. The table uses UWA's published conservation tariff for foreign non-residents.

ActivityMinimum ageFee per person (foreign non-resident)
Gorilla trekking, Bwindi or Mgahinga15US$800
Chimpanzee tracking, Kibale12US$250
Park entry, Bwindi, Kibale or Queen ElizabethNoneUS$40 adult, US$20 child aged 5-15, under-5s free
Launch cruise, Queen ElizabethNone setUS$30
Guided short nature walk for children (Bwindi, Mgahinga, Kibale)ChildrenUS$5

Fees are from UWA's tariff for January 2027 to June 2028, checked November 2026. UWA revises its rates every couple of years, so confirm the figures in your quote before booking. Low-season rates apply only in April, May and November.

What younger children do while others trek

On any Uganda family safari, the days when the over-15s go to the gorillas are the ones to plan most carefully. In Kibale, younger children can join the Bigodi Wetland walk, a community-run sanctuary with monkeys and birds. In Bwindi, UWA lists short guided nature walks for children, and many families pair the trek day with a Batwa community visit that everyone can join in the afternoon.

Someone has to stay with the youngest. Often a grandparent who would rather not climb is happy to do it; otherwise your driver guide or the lodge can help, but agree this in advance rather than on the morning. Tell us every traveller's age when you ask for a quote and we will check eligibility before any permit is bought.

For the over-15s, the trek itself takes one to six hours on steep, muddy slopes, depending on where the gorillas have moved overnight. Our post on how hard gorilla trekking is explains fitness, porters and how rangers try to give slower walkers a closer gorilla family.

A Route That Works for Mixed Ages

The Uganda family safari route that suits most groups runs Entebbe, Kibale, Queen Elizabeth, Bwindi and back, over seven to ten days. It puts the chimpanzees before the gorillas, so teenagers get used to forest walking first, and it breaks the long drive south into manageable pieces.

Kibale Forest and Bigodi (two nights)

Kibale is about 350 km from Entebbe, a drive of five to six hours, so day one or two is mostly road. Break it with lunch and plan an easy afternoon. The next morning the over-12s track chimpanzees while younger children do the Bigodi walk; our guide to chimpanzee trekking in Kibale covers the morning and afternoon slots.

Queen Elizabeth National Park and Ishasha (one or two nights)

Queen Elizabeth is two to three hours south of Kibale past crater lakes. This is the most child-friendly stop on a Uganda family safari: an afternoon launch on the Kazinga Channel among hippos and elephants, morning game drives, and in the southern Ishasha sector a good chance of lions lying in fig trees. Two nights here gives younger children a rest from early starts.

Bwindi Impenetrable National Park (two nights)

The drive from Queen Elizabeth to Buhoma in northern Bwindi via Ishasha takes around five to six hours, and the Ishasha road can be hard going in heavy rain. Two nights in Bwindi gives a buffer if weather or fitness pushes the trek back. Read our Bwindi gorilla trekking guide for the four sectors and how permits are allocated.

The return from Bwindi to Entebbe is roughly eight to nine hours by road. With young children or older relatives, a domestic flight from an airstrip near Bwindi back to Entebbe is often worth the extra cost, and we can price both options side by side.

Vehicles, Rooms and Splitting the Group

Vehicles and rooms decide whether a Uganda family safari for several households feels relaxed or crowded. Uganda's 4x4 safari vehicles usually seat six to seven passengers with a window each, and lodges near the parks are small, so a group of ten or more needs early bookings and a clear plan.

A vehicle plan for a Uganda family safari

The simplest rule is one vehicle per household, or per six people. Two families of four fit better in two vehicles than squeezed into one, because each family can stop when a child needs a break, and the vehicles regroup at lunch and the lodge. Bring car seats or booster seats from home for small children, and tell us so we know which vehicle they go in.

Rooms for grandparents, parents and teenagers

For a Uganda family safari, family rooms and interconnecting rooms are limited in Kibale and Bwindi, and they go first in July, August and over Christmas. Many groups mix room types: grandparents in a quieter room near the main area, parents with young children in a family unit, and teenage cousins sharing. Ask for rooms close to the dining area if anyone has mobility concerns, because lodges on Bwindi's slopes can involve steps.

Gorilla permits add one more twist. Each habituated gorilla family takes eight visitors a day, so a party of eleven eligible trekkers will be split across two gorilla families, sometimes in different parts of the sector. Our post on group gorilla trekking in Uganda explains how larger parties are divided.

How Much Does a Uganda Family Safari Cost for a Group?

The cost of a Uganda family safari for a group comes down to three things: permits for eligible travellers, lodge level and vehicle numbers. Permits and park fees are fixed per person, while vehicles and driver guides are shared, so each extra traveller in a vehicle lowers the cost per head.

The fixed part is easy to work out. On UWA's 2027-2028 tariff, a 16-year-old pays the same US$800 gorilla permit and US$250 chimpanzee permit as an adult. A ten-year-old pays neither, plus reduced park entry. A family of two adults and two children aged 10 and 13 therefore needs two gorilla permits and three chimpanzee permits, not four of each.

TravellerGorilla permitChimpanzee permit
AdultYes, US$800Yes, US$250
Teenager aged 15-17Yes, US$800Yes, US$250
Child aged 12-14Not allowedYes, US$250
Child under 12Not allowedNot allowed

Lodges are the variable part of Uganda family safari pricing. Uganda has comfortable mid-range lodges and a handful of high-end ones near Bwindi and Kibale, and child rates differ from lodge to lodge, so we confirm them in each quote rather than guessing. Domestic flights, porters and tips are extra.

For groups, our 7 day Uganda family gorilla safari gives every seventh place free for each six paying travellers, families can pay separately, and a deposit of 30 to 40% holds the booking. Price is on request because it depends on dates, ages and rooms.

Health, Safety and Paperwork for Families

Health and paperwork for a Uganda family safari are manageable if you start eight weeks out. Malaria is the main health risk for children and adults, so every traveller should see a travel clinic for antimalarials and vaccines, and pack repellent, long sleeves and trousers for evenings.

On entry rules, Uganda's Ministry of Internal Affairs said in October 2026 that a yellow fever certificate is not a condition of entry. Health services may still recommend the vaccine, and if you route through Kenya or another country you may need it there, so check our yellow fever requirements for Kenya and Tanzania if you are combining countries. Visas are applied for online; if you are adding Kenya or Rwanda, the East Africa Tourist Visa can cover all three.

Safety on a Uganda family safari is mostly about pace and supervision. Guides control every game drive and walk, but children must stay seated in the vehicle and close to adults at lodges without fences. Our safe family safari planning post covers rules for children in the bush, and every traveller should carry travel insurance that covers trekking and medical evacuation.

When Is the Best Time to Bring the Family?

The best time for a Uganda family safari is June to August or December to February. These are Uganda's drier months, trails in Kibale and Bwindi are less slippery, the Ishasha road is easier, and they line up with summer and Christmas school holidays in Europe and North America.

Those months are also the busiest, so gorilla permits for a large party on one date need booking well ahead. March to May and October to November bring more rain, though forests stay green and showers often pass in an hour or two. UWA applies low-season permit rates in April, May and November, which matters when you are buying eight or ten permits.

A Uganda family safari at Easter or in late October suits a family that wants quieter lodges and can accept muddier treks. Whatever the month, the Uganda safari packages page lists other routes, such as adding Lake Mburo or Murchison Falls for a longer trip.

Insider Tips

  • Collect ages first: Ask every household for passport names and dates of birth before anyone talks about lodges
  • Plan the stay-behind day: Decide who stays with under-15s on gorilla day and what they will do
  • Two nights in Bwindi: Gives a spare day if rain or fitness delays the trek
  • One vehicle per household: Keeps each family's pace and stops arguments over window seats
  • Fly back from Bwindi: Saves an eight-to-nine-hour drive for small children and grandparents
  • Pack for the forest: Long trousers, gardening gloves, waterproofs and boots with grip for anyone trekking

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the minimum age for gorilla trekking on a Uganda family safari?

The minimum age for gorilla trekking on a Uganda family safari is 15, set by the Uganda Wildlife Authority, and chimpanzee tracking in Kibale starts at 12. Rangers check ages, so bring passports. Younger children still enjoy the trip: they join boat cruises, game drives, community visits and short guided children's walks while older relatives trek.

How many people can share a Uganda family safari vehicle?

Most Uganda safari vehicles seat six to seven passengers with a window each, plus the driver guide. For a Uganda family safari with more than six people, two or more vehicles work better than one large one: each family keeps its own pace, nobody sits in a middle seat, and the vehicles meet at lodges and activity starts.

Is a Uganda family safari safe for young children?

A Uganda family safari is a reasonable choice for young children when it is planned with care: antimalarial advice from a travel clinic, repellent and long sleeves at dusk, shorter driving days and lodges that accept children. The main risks are malaria, long road days and sun, not wildlife, because guides control every game drive and walk.

When is the best time for a family safari in Uganda?

June to August and December to February are the driest months in Uganda and match most school holidays, so trails are easier and roads faster. Gorillas and chimpanzees can be seen all year. April, May and November are wetter, but the Uganda Wildlife Authority applies low-season permit rates in those months, so flexible families can save.

How far ahead should several families book a Uganda gorilla safari?

Several families travelling together should book six to twelve months ahead, and earlier for July, August and Christmas. Each gorilla family takes only eight visitors a day, so a large group needs permits on the same date, sometimes split across two gorilla families or sectors. Permits are only secured once paid in full.

Final Thoughts

A Uganda family safari shared by several households works when the ages drive the plan: chimpanzees from 12, gorillas from 15, and a proper programme for everyone else on those days. Add one vehicle per household, two nights in Bwindi and the dry months if you can, and the trip suits toddlers and grandparents alike.
